problems.title: Pair Sum in a Sorted List
problems.statement:
You get a list of integers `nums` sorted from smallest to largest, and a number `target`.
Find the two different positions whose values add up to `target` and return them as `[i, j]` with `i < j`.

Exactly one such pair exists.
hints: Because the list is sorted, a sum that is too small can only grow by moving the left side right.
Start one pointer at each end.

approaches.name: Two Pointers
approaches.idea:
Put one pointer, L, on the smallest number and another, R, on the largest.

If their sum is too small, the only way to grow it is to move L to the right. If it is too big, move R to the left. Each step throws away one number that can never be part of the answer.

problems.title: Palindrome After Cleanup
problems.statement:
A phrase counts as a palindrome if, after you ignore everything that is not a letter or a digit and treat
uppercase and lowercase as equal, it reads the same forwards and backwards.

Given a string `s`, return `true` if it is a palindrome under these rules.
hints: Compare characters from both ends.
Skip anything that is not a letter or digit before comparing.

approaches.idea:
Put L at the start and R at the end. Skip over punctuation and spaces on either side.

When both point at letters or digits, compare them ignoring case. Any mismatch means it is not a palindrome. If the pointers meet, it is.

non-zero numbers keep their original relative order.

approaches.idea:
Use a read pointer R that scans every number, and a write pointer W that marks where the next non-zero number should go.

Each time R finds a non-zero number, swap it into position W and move W forward. Zeros naturally drift to the end.

problems.title: Remove Repeats From a Sorted List
problems.statement:
`nums` is sorted in non-decreasing order. Remove the repeated values **in place** so each distinct value appears
once, keeping the order. Return `k`, the number of distinct values; the first `k` slots of `nums` must hold them.

examples.why: k = 2 and the array starts with 1, 2.

hints: Duplicates are next to each other in a sorted array.
Write each new value at a write pointer.

approaches.name: Two Pointers (read & write)
approaches.idea:
The first value is always kept, so the write pointer W starts at 1. The read pointer R scans the rest.

Whenever R sees a value different from the last kept one, copy it to W and move W forward. At the end, W is the count of distinct values.

`nums` is sorted. Remove extra copies **in place** so every value appears at most twice, keeping the order.

hints: Compare the new value with the one written two slots back.

problems.title: Merge Two Sorted Lists Into the First
problems.statement:
`a` has length `m + n`: its first `m` values are sorted and the last `n` slots are zeros (free space).
`b` holds `n` sorted values. Merge `b` into `a` **in place** so that `a` becomes fully sorted.
hints: Filling from the front would overwrite values you still need.
Fill from the back with the larger of the two tails.

approaches.name: Two Pointers from the back
approaches.idea:
The free space is at the end of `a`, so fill the result from the back. I points at the last real value of `a`, J at the last value of `b`, and K at the slot to fill.

Put the larger of the two tails into slot K and move that pointer left. When `b` runs out, everything left in `a` is already in place.

Return every distinct triple of values `[a, b, c]` from `nums` (using three different positions) with
`a + b + c = 0`. No triple may appear twice. Any order is accepted.
hints: Sort the numbers first.
Fix the first value, then solve a two-pointer pair sum on the rest.

approaches.idea:
Sort the array. Fix the first number of the triple, then look for two numbers to its right that add up to minus that number, using L and R from both ends.

Skip values equal to the previous one so the same triple is never reported twice.

that sum. Exactly one closest sum exists.

approaches.idea:
Sort, fix the first value, and use L and R on the remaining range. If the current sum is below the target, move L right to grow it; if above, move R left.

Remember whichever sum has been closest so far, and stop early on an exact hit.

Three reversals do the trick.

The first reversal moves the last k values to the front (backwards); the next two put each part back in the right order.

`people[i]` is the weight of person `i`. Each boat carries at most two people and at most `limit` total weight.

Given positive integers `nums` and a positive number `s`, return the length of the shortest contiguous run whose
sum is **at least** `s`, or `0` if no run reaches it.

Then, while the sum is at least `s`, record the window length and shrink from the left: subtract `nums[left]` and move `left` forward. The sentinel `n + 1` means "no window found yet".

problems.statement:

approaches.idea:
The answer at i is the product of everything to its left times everything to its right.

First sweep left to right, writing the running product of the left side into the result. Then sweep right to left with a second running product for the right side, multiplying it in.

def product_except_self(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    res = [1] * n
    left = 1
    for i in range(n):
        res[i] = left
        left *= nums[i]
    right = 1
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        res[i] *= right
        right *= nums[i]
    return res

problems.statement: Return the number of contiguous subarrays of `nums` whose sum equals `k`. Values may be negative.

approaches.name: Prefix Sum + Hash Map
approaches.idea:
Keep the running prefix sum. A run ending here sums to k exactly when some earlier prefix equals current − k.

    seen, prefix, count = {0: 1}, 0, 0

def divisible_runs(nums, k):
    seen = [0] * k
    seen[0] = 1
    rem = count = 0
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):

        count += seen[rem]

    return count

def rotate_chain(head, k):
    if not head:
        return head
    n, tail = 1, head
    while tail.next:
        tail, n = tail.next, n + 1
    k %= n
    tail.next = head
    new_tail = head
    for _ in range(n - k - 1):
        new_tail = new_tail.next
    new_head = new_tail.next
    new_tail.next = None
    return new_head

from collections import deque

def levels(root):
    res, q = [], deque([root] if root else [])
    while q:
        level = []
        for _ in range(len(q)):
            node = q.popleft()
            level.append(node.val)
            q.extend(c for c in (node.left, node.right) if c)
        res.append(level)

import heapq

def merge_k(lists):
    heap = [(node.val, i, node) for i, node in enumerate(lists) if node]
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    dummy = tail = ListNode()
    while heap:
        val, i, node = heapq.heappop(heap)
        tail.next = node
        tail = node
        if node.next:
            heapq.heappush(heap, (node.next.val, i, node.next))
    return dummy.next

def insert(intervals, new):
    res, i, n = [], 0, len(intervals)
    start, end = new
    while i < n and intervals[i][1] < start:

        i += 1

problems.title: Can Every Course Be Taken?
problems.statement:
There are `n` courses numbered `0..n−1`. Each pair `[a, b]` in `prereqs` means course `b` must be taken before
course `a`. Return `true` if it's possible to finish every course (no circular requirements).

examples.why: Each course needs the other first.

hints: Count each course's unmet prerequisites (in-degree).
Repeatedly take courses whose count is zero.

approaches.name: Kahn's Topological Sort
approaches.idea:
Count each course's unmet prerequisites. Courses with none can be taken now: put them in a queue. Taking a course reduces the count of every course that depends on it, possibly freeing new ones.

If every course eventually gets taken, there's no cycle.

code.name: solution.py
code.src:
from collections import deque

def can_finish(n, prereqs):
    adj, indeg = [[] for _ in range(n)], [0] * n
    for a, b in prereqs:
        adj[b].append(a)
        indeg[a] += 1
    q = deque(i for i in range(n) if indeg[i] == 0)
    taken, taken_set = 0, set()
    while q:
        c = q.popleft()
        taken += 1
        taken_set.add(c)
        for nxt in adj[c]:
            indeg[nxt] -= 1
            if indeg[nxt] == 0:
                q.append(nxt)
    return taken == n

import heapq

def course_order(n, prereqs):
    adj, indeg = [[] for _ in range(n)], [0] * n
    for a, b in prereqs:
        adj[b].append(a)
        indeg[a] += 1
    heap = [i for i in range(n) if indeg[i] == 0]
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    order = []
    while heap:
        c = heapq.heappop(heap)
        order.append(c)
        for nxt in adj[c]:
            indeg[nxt] -= 1
            if indeg[nxt] == 0:
                heapq.heappush(heap, nxt)
    return order if len(order) == n else []

def max_product(nums):
    hi = lo = best = nums[0]
    for i in range(1, len(nums)):
        x = nums[i]
        hi, lo = max(x, hi * x, lo * x), min(x, hi * x, lo * x)
        best = max(best, hi)
    return best

def spiral(matrix):
    res = []
    top, bottom, left, right = 0, len(matrix) - 1, 0, len(matrix[0]) - 1
    while top <= bottom and left <= right:
        res += [matrix[top][c] for c in range(left, right + 1)]
        top += 1
        res += [matrix[r][right] for r in range(top, bottom + 1)]
        right -= 1
        if top <= bottom:
            res += [matrix[bottom][c] for c in range(right, left - 1, -1)]
            bottom -= 1
        if left <= right:
            res += [matrix[r][left] for r in range(bottom, top - 1, -1)]
            left += 1
    return res

problems.statement:
Semantic search compares a `query` embedding with stored `vectors` using cosine similarity
(dot product divided by the product of lengths). Return the indices of the `k` most similar vectors, most similar

constraints: all vectors share the same dimension

approaches.name: Min-Heap of Size k
approaches.idea:
Compute each vector's cosine similarity with the query. Keep a min-heap holding the best k so far: if a new score beats the smallest in the heap, replace it.

import heapq
import math

def top_k_similar(vectors, query, k):
    qn = math.sqrt(sum(x * x for x in query))
    scores, heap = [], []
    for i, v in enumerate(vectors):
        dot = sum(a * b for a, b in zip(v, query))
        scores.append(dot / (math.sqrt(sum(a * a for a in v)) * qn))
        heapq.heappush(heap, (scores[-1], -i))
        if len(heap) > k:
            heapq.heappop(heap)
    return [-n for s, n in sorted(heap, reverse=True)]

import math

def softmax(logits):
    m = max(logits)
    exps = [math.exp(x - m) for x in logits]
    total = sum(exps)
    return [e / total for e in exps]

import heapq

def merge_shards(shards, n):
    heap = [(-s[0], i, 0) for i, s in enumerate(shards) if s]
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    res = []
    while heap and len(res) < n:
        neg, i, j = heapq.heappop(heap)
        res.append(-neg)
        if j + 1 < len(shards[i]):
            heapq.heappush(heap, (-shards[i][j + 1], i, j + 1))
    return res

problems.statement:
Protect an AI endpoint: each `X-API-Key` may make at most 60 requests in any rolling 60 seconds. Extra requests get
**429 Too Many Requests** with a `Retry-After` header. Implement it as a servlet filter using the sliding-window log
idea, safe under concurrent requests.

examples.in: 61st request from key K within 60 s

hints: Keep a deque of request timestamps per key.
Synchronise on the per-key deque, not on the whole filter.

approaches.name: OncePerRequestFilter + per-key deque
approaches.idea:
This is the sliding-window algorithm from the Practice tab, inside a real web filter. Each API key owns a deque of request times. On each request, drop timestamps older than the window from the front; if the deque is still full, reject with 429.

Locking only the key's own deque keeps different clients from blocking each other. In a multi-instance deployment you'd move this state to Redis.

problems.title: Caching Expensive Embedding Calls
problems.statement:
Computing a text embedding costs money and ~200 ms. Cache embeddings by input text so repeated texts are free, and
provide a way to evict a single entry when the model changes.

examples.out: first call hits the model; second returns from cache

hints: `@EnableCaching` plus `@Cacheable` on the service method.
Only calls through the Spring proxy are cached.

approaches.name: @Cacheable / @CacheEvict
approaches.idea:
`@Cacheable("embeddings")` checks the cache before running the method, keyed by its argument; on a miss it runs the method and stores the result.

Caching works through a Spring proxy, so calling the method from inside the same class bypasses the cache. In production you'd back it with Caffeine or Redis and set a size or time limit.

problems.title: Calling Services in Parallel
problems.statement:
A dashboard needs a user's profile (300 ms) and recommendations (500 ms) from two services. Fetch both concurrently
so the total is about 500 ms, with a 2-second overall timeout.
hints: `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync` runs work on an executor.
Java 21 virtual threads make blocking calls cheap.

approaches.name: CompletableFuture + virtual threads
approaches.idea:
Start both calls with `supplyAsync` on a virtual-thread executor, then combine them with `thenCombine` once both finish. `orTimeout` fails the whole request if it takes too long.

Virtual threads (Java 21) let blocking HTTP calls scale without a big thread pool; Spring Boot can also enable them globally with `spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true`.

problems.title: Resilient LLM API Client
problems.statement:
Call an LLM completion API with Spring's `RestClient`: send the prompt as JSON, read the answer, apply timeouts,
and retry up to 3 times with exponential backoff (500 ms, 1 s, 2 s) on HTTP 429 or 5xx, never on other 4xx errors.

examples.out: returns the answer after one retry

hints: Only retry errors that are likely temporary.
Back off exponentially to avoid hammering a struggling service.

approaches.name: RestClient + backoff loop
approaches.idea:
`RestClient` is Spring's modern synchronous HTTP client with a fluent API. Configure base URL and timeouts once, then each call is a short chain.

Retry only transient failures: 429 (rate limited) and 5xx (server problems). Client errors like 400 won't fix themselves. Doubling the delay each time (exponential backoff) gives the service room to recover.

problems.title: Streaming LLM Tokens With Server-Sent Events
problems.statement:
Users shouldn't stare at a spinner while a model writes a long answer. Expose `GET /api/chat/stream?q=...` that
streams each generated token to the browser as a Server-Sent Event, then sends a final `done` event.
hints: `SseEmitter` keeps the HTTP response open and sends events.
Generate on another thread so the request thread is freed.

approaches.name: SseEmitter on a virtual thread
approaches.idea:
`SseEmitter` holds the response open and lets you push events with `send`. Run the generation on a separate (virtual) thread: for each token from the model, send a `token` event; finish with a `done` event and `complete()`.

If the client disconnects, `send` throws, so stop and call `completeWithError` to free resources.

problems.title: Idempotent Payments With an Idempotency Key
problems.statement:
Mobile clients retry `POST /api/payments` when the network drops, which must never charge twice. Require an
`Idempotency-Key` header: the first request with a key is processed; any retry with the same key returns the
original result without charging again, even if two retries arrive at the same time.
hints: Store results by key.
`ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent` runs the work at most once per key.

approaches.name: computeIfAbsent result store
approaches.idea:
Keep a map from idempotency key to the payment result. `computeIfAbsent` atomically runs the charge only for the first request with a key; concurrent duplicates wait and receive the same stored result.

In production this map lives in a database table with a unique constraint on the key, plus an expiry policy.

problems.title: Testing a Controller With MockMvc
problems.statement:
Write fast slice tests for `GreetingController` (which delegates to a `GreetingService`): one checks the JSON body
of a successful call, another checks that a blank name returns 400. Mock the service.
hints: `@WebMvcTest` loads only the web layer.
`@MockitoBean` replaces the service with a Mockito mock.

approaches.name: @WebMvcTest + MockMvc + @MockitoBean
approaches.idea:
`@WebMvcTest` starts only the MVC slice (controllers, advice, JSON), which makes tests much faster than a full `@SpringBootTest`. `MockMvc` performs requests without a real server, and `@MockitoBean` swaps the service for a mock you control.

Assert on status and on JSON fields with JsonPath expressions.

health indicator that reports `DOWN` (with details) when the model server's ping fails.

problems.title: A Counter With Signals
problems.statement:
Build a standalone `CounterComponent` with + / − / reset buttons. Show the count and a derived label
("even"/"odd") that updates automatically.
hints: `signal()` holds state; `computed()` derives from it.
Read a signal by calling it: `count()`.

approaches.name: signal + computed
approaches.idea:
A `signal` is a reactive value: reading it in the template subscribes the view, and `set`/`update` notify it. `computed` derives a value from other signals and recalculates only when they change.

No subscriptions, no manual change detection, and it works in zoneless apps.

problems.title: Parent and Child: Inputs and Outputs
problems.statement:
Create a reusable `StarRatingComponent` that receives the current `rating` (required) and `max` (default 5) from
its parent, renders clickable stars, and emits `rated` with the chosen value.
hints: `input.required<number>()` declares a required signal input.
`output<number>()` declares an event.

approaches.name: input() / output()
approaches.idea:
Signal inputs (`input()`, `input.required()`) receive data from the parent and are read like signals. `output()` creates an event the parent listens to with `( )` binding.

Data flows down through inputs and events flow up through outputs, which keeps components reusable.

Render a task list: show a loading message while loading, each task with a ✓ when done, an empty-state message when

problems.title: Sign-Up Form With Validation
problems.statement:
Build a sign-up form with email (required, valid), password (min 8 chars) and confirm-password fields. Show
errors only after a field is touched, add a custom "passwords match" validator, and disable submit while invalid.
hints: Use a typed `NonNullableFormBuilder`.
A group-level validator can compare two controls.

approaches.name: Typed Reactive Forms
approaches.idea:
Reactive forms model the form in TypeScript, which makes validation logic testable and type-safe. `NonNullableFormBuilder` gives strongly typed controls whose values are never null.

A custom validator on the group compares password and confirmation, and the template shows messages only for touched controls.

problems.title: A Typed HTTP Data Service
problems.statement:
Create a `ProductService` that loads `/api/products` with `HttpClient`, returns typed data, and falls back to an
empty list (while logging) when the request fails. Show the products in a component as a signal.

examples.out: component shows an empty list, error logged

hints: `inject(HttpClient)` inside an `@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })` service.
`toSignal` converts an Observable into a signal.

approaches.name: Injectable service + toSignal
approaches.idea:
Keep HTTP logic in a root-provided service so components stay simple and the service is easy to mock. `catchError` turns failures into a safe fallback value.

In the component, `toSignal` subscribes to the Observable for you and exposes the latest value as a signal, unsubscribing automatically.

problems.title: Debounced Search Box
problems.statement:
Search as the user types, without sending a request for every keystroke: wait until typing pauses for 300 ms,
skip repeated terms, ignore terms shorter than 2 characters, and cancel stale requests when a new term arrives.
hints: `debounceTime`, `distinctUntilChanged`, `filter`, `switchMap`.

approaches.name: RxJS pipeline + switchMap
approaches.idea: A `FormControl`'s `valueChanges` is a stream of keystrokes. `debounceTime` waits for a pause, `distinctUntilChanged` drops repeats, and `switchMap` cancels the previous HTTP request whenever a new term arrives, so stale results can't overwrite fresh ones.

problems.title: Protecting Routes With a Guard
problems.statement:
Only signed-in users may open `/account`. Write a functional route guard that lets authenticated users through and
redirects everyone else to `/login?returnUrl=...`.
hints: A `CanActivateFn` can `inject()` services.
Return a `UrlTree` to redirect.

approaches.name: Functional CanActivateFn
approaches.idea:
Guards are plain functions in modern Angular. `inject()` works inside them, so the guard can read the auth state and return either `true` or a `UrlTree` that redirects, which is safer than calling `navigate` inside a guard.

Guards are a UX convenience: the server must still enforce permissions.

problems.title: HTTP Interceptor for Tokens and Retries
problems.statement:
Every API call needs `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. Write a functional HTTP interceptor that adds the header to
requests for `/api`, retries GET requests twice on network or 503 errors with a short delay, and register it.

examples.out: sent with Authorization header; retried on 503

hints: `HttpInterceptorFn` receives `req` and `next`.
Requests are immutable: use `req.clone`.

approaches.name: HttpInterceptorFn + retry
approaches.idea: Interceptors sit between your code and the network. Since requests are immutable, clone the request with the extra header. RxJS `retry` with a delay function re-subscribes on failure; limit it to safe, idempotent GET requests and to errors that are worth retrying.

problems.title: A Shopping Cart Store With Signals
problems.statement:
Manage cart state in a service: add items (merging quantities), remove items, and expose derived totals that every
component can read. Keep the state read-only from outside.

examples.out: one line: apple ×3; total updates everywhere

hints: Private writable signal, public `asReadonly()`.
Derived values are `computed`.

approaches.name: Service store with signals
approaches.idea:
A root service owns a private writable signal and exposes a read-only view. Methods describe the allowed changes and compute new immutable arrays, while `computed` values such as the total update automatically.

This covers most app state needs before reaching for a state library.

problems.title: Faster Loads With Lazy Routes and @defer
problems.statement:
Cut the initial bundle: lazy-load the admin area only when visited, and defer rendering a heavy chart component
until it scrolls into view, with a placeholder and loading state.

examples.out: admin and chart code are not downloaded yet

hints: `loadComponent` / `loadChildren` with dynamic `import()`.
`@defer (on viewport)` with `@placeholder` and `@loading`.

approaches.name: loadComponent + @defer
approaches.idea:
A route's `loadComponent` uses a dynamic `import()`, so its code becomes a separate chunk fetched on first navigation.

Inside templates, `@defer` lazily loads the components in its block when a trigger fires, such as `on viewport`, and shows `@placeholder` and `@loading` content meanwhile.

problems.title: Streaming AI Chat UI
problems.statement:
Build a chat component that sends a question to `/api/chat/stream?q=...` (Server-Sent Events) and renders the
answer token by token as it arrives, disables input while streaming, and closes the stream when done or destroyed.

examples.out: the answer appears word by word; the input re-enables at the end

hints: `EventSource` receives named SSE events.
Append tokens to a signal; clean up in `DestroyRef.onDestroy`.

approaches.name: EventSource + signals
approaches.idea:
The browser's `EventSource` connects to an SSE endpoint and fires a handler per named event. Each `token` event appends text to an `answer` signal, so the view updates live. The `done` event, an error, or the component being destroyed closes the connection.

This pairs with the Spring Boot SSE exercise to give an end-to-end streaming LLM feature.
